q: How many minutes fit on one side of a vinyl record?
a: It depends on size, speed and the music. One US plant suggests 18 to 20 minutes for a 12-inch at 33 1/3 rpm and 12 to 14 at 45, while a Danish plant allows up to 15 minutes at 45 and 5 on a 7-inch. Quiet, lightly compressed music can run longer.

q: Why does bass need to be mono for vinyl?
a: Differences between the left and right channels move the groove up and down, and big low-frequency differences make big vertical swings that can cause skipping. Plants advise centering bass, though at least one veteran cutting engineer found that skipping the mono filter often sounded fuller.

It is the standard EQ for records, set in 1954: the cut reduces bass and boosts treble, and the playback stage reverses it so the result is flat. It keeps bass from hogging groove space and improves signal-to-noise.

q: Why does the end of a record side sound worse?
a: The groove moves slower near the label, about 7.4 inches per second against almost 21 at the rim on a 12-inch LP, so wavelengths get shorter and harder to track. Loud, bright passages suffer most, which is why quiet songs often close a side.

q: What does DMM mean on a vinyl record?
a: Direct Metal Mastering cuts the groove into copper on a stainless steel disc instead of lacquer, and the cut disc acts as the mother for plating. Teldec claims more playing time and less noise; some listeners hear DMM as bright.
The source and lathe both run at half speed, so an LP is cut at about 16 2/3 rpm, giving the stylus more time for high frequencies. It needs modified EQ and takes about four times as long per cut.
A record cut one at a time in real time into a blank, with no plating or pressing. Sellers pitch it for one copy up to a few dozen, with lower and more variable fidelity than pressed vinyl.
